Beyond Accuracy: What Are Speech Emotion Recognition Models Learning?
abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is important in human-machine interactions, enabling machines to detect and classify human emotions from solely human speech. Speech emotion recognition (SER) benchmarks routinely report accuracies above 90 percent, yet these models fail when deployed or tested on diverse speakers. The papers overlook a fundamental issue: models may be learning speaker identity and tone rather than generalized emotional cues. We introduce a two-condition audit protocol that measures, for any published SER model, how much of its reported performance survives when speakers are held out. Each model is evaluated twice under identical architecture, features, and training recipe: a control condition that reproduces the common random-split practice, and a strict speaker-independent condition with disjoint speakers. We apply the protocol to seven model configurations from five published papers, spanning convolutional, recurrent, transformer, vision-transformer, and self-supervised wav2vec2 architectures, on RAVDESS, EMO-DB, and SAVEE, with a fourth corpus (EARS) as an external check. Across 21 model-dataset pairs, published headline numbers reproduce close to the control but drop by 6.9 to 63.1 percentage points under strict speaker independence. Our results quantify speaker memorization as a dominant, previously unmeasured component of published SER performance, and we recommend two-condition reporting as a community standard.

title: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps
abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.

title: Cross-Scale Sparse Attention for Referring Segmentation in Remote Sensing
abstract: High-resolution remote sensing (RS) imagery provides fine spatial detail over large areas, making it essential for fine-grained scene understanding. Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation (RRSIS) aims to segment regions described by natural language, yet many existing methods rely on sequential alignment--fusion pipelines with limited joint modeling of cross-scale visual hierarchies and linguistic dependencies. Moreover, dense attention mechanisms struggle with the sparsity and wide spatial dispersion of RS targets, while current datasets offer limited structured evaluation of multi-target references, multi-hop relational reasoning, and multi-granularity descriptions, limiting both model development and evaluation. To address these challenges, we propose a Cross-Scale Sparse Attention Model (CSSAM), which aligns multiscale visual features with complex referring expressions through two key modules. The Cross-scale Modality-aligned Fusion Module (CMFM) performs unified cross-scale cross-modal fusion, while the Dynamic Multimodal Sparse Hybrid Attention (DMSHA) selectively attends to informative visual--textual tokens, reducing dense visual interactions. Furthermore, we introduce M$^{3}$RRSIS-D, a RRSIS dataset explicitly designed around three core reasoning dimensions: multi-target (M$^{1}$), reference-dependent multi-hop (M$^{2}$), and multi-granularity (M$^{3}$) expressions. Extensive experiments on M$^{3}$RRSIS-D and two public RRSIS benchmarks demonstrate that CSSAM achieves competitive performance across accuracy, fine-grained reasoning, and high-IoU localization metrics, validating its effectiveness for complex semantic reasoning in realistic RS scenarios. Code, dataset, and model weights will be released upon acceptance.

title: Promise and Limits of Cross-Architecture Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Medical Vision Transformers (LiteMed-ViT)
abstract: Running deep models for medical image analysis at the point of care is challenging with standard architectures: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are often too heavy for edge devices, while Vision Transformers (ViTs) require massive training datasets to compensate for missing inductive biases. This study investigates how far the dual-token distillation used to train data-efficient ViTs can be pushed when applied across architectures, from a CNN-based teacher into a lightweight ViT student. LiteMed-ViT is introduced as a dual-token ViT featuring a convolutional stem and a class-balanced distillation objective; at 0.234M parameters, LiteMed-ViT carries 47.8x fewer parameters than its ResNet18 teacher at a memory footprint of just 0.89 MB. Evaluated against three compact CNN baselines on three MedMNIST subsets of varying modality and class balance, LiteMed-ViT attains higher accuracy than all three baselines on BloodMNIST (95.05%) and two on PathMNIST (89.15%). Under MedMNIST-C corruptions, it is at least as robust as every compact CNN across all subsets, outperforming them on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST without declining in relative standing as severity increases. Particular attention is devoted to identifying the exact conditions where performance plateaus. On DermaMNIST, LiteMed-ViT's balanced accuracy remains up to 1.9 points below the strongest compact CNNs and does not benefit from higher input resolutions up to 224 pixels, where ResNet18 gains 12.6 points. Stronger teachers do not yield a more accurate student, and overconfident ones lower its DermaMNIST balanced accuracy unless calibrated.

title: Component Pooling Trained Across Orientations for Few-Shot Remote Sensing Scene Classification
abstract: Few-shot remote sensing scene classification (FSRSSC) aims to recognize novel scene categories from only a few labeled images. Most FSRSSC methods summarize the feature map of an image by global average pooling, which treats the few objects that define an aerial scene and the large background around them alike, and they rarely consider that aerial images have no canonical orientation. To address these issues, we propose RoCoP, a parameter-free component pooling network trained across orientations. RoCoP consists of a feature extractor, a non-negative decomposition module (NDM) and a component scoring module (CSM). NDM factorizes the local descriptors of each image into a few additive components with a deterministic initialization and a single multiplicative update, so that the positions of one object are grouped together. CSM weights each component by its activation magnitude and converts the weights into a soft mask for pooling. Because both modules are invariant to permutations of feature positions, the only rotation-sensitive part of the pipeline is the backbone, which we train to classify randomly rotated views of every image. Experiments on NWPU-RESISC45, AID and UC Merced show that component pooling and rotated-view training are complementary: together they improve a strong transfer-learning baseline by about 2.5 points in 5-way 1-shot accuracy on NWPU-RESISC45 and AID, without adding parameters at inference. Under an identical protocol, RoCoP outperforms re-implemented metric-based and task-adaptive methods, and NDM and CSM also improve existing methods when plugged into them. We further identify the regime in which the method does not apply, namely very small base sets.

title: FreqPKC: Frequency-Aware PeakConv for Radar Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Automotive millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar has attracted increasing attention for semantic segmentation in autonomous driving, owing to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent works have introduced radar-specific neural operators such as PeakConv (PKC), inspired by constant false alarm rate (CFAR) detection, to better model the peak-dominated characteristics of radar images. However, existing methods typically treat the guard bandwidth as learnable parameters, without explicitly characterizing the frequency response of the PKC operator. In this work, we revisit PKC from a frequency-domain perspective and propose Frequency-Aware PeakConv (FreqPKC), which explicitly models and exploits its underlying spectral characteristics. By analyzing the frequency response of PKC, FreqPKC enables the network to capture a broader range of frequency components and adaptively adjust its effective bandwidth. With the proposed Frequency-Aware (FA) module, the network can infer appropriate guard bandwidths to balance high- and low-frequency information: it enhances high-frequency components in target regions for more precise segmentation while suppressing noise through low-frequency filtering in background areas. Building on FreqPKC, we further develop FreqPKC-Net, a radar semantic segmentation (RSS) framework that integrates frequency-guided adaptive modulation with cross-view fusion for multi-view inputs, and can also be adapted to single-view data. Experiments on the public datasets CARRADA, CARRADA-RAC, and a self-built dataset named RS-SAR demonstrate that FreqPKC-Net consistently outperforms existing SoTA methods on both range-Doppler and range-angle views.

title: Dynamic Query as Budgeting for Tiny Object Detection
abstract: Recent DETR-based tiny object detectors adopt dynamic query mechanisms to handle severe density imbalance. However, existing designs entangle two effects: how many and which queries are decoded. This entanglement obscures what drives the gains and complicates dynamic-query design; additional learned predictors and heuristic filtering also introduce overhead and potential selection errors. We disentangle these effects and show that dynamic query primarily acts as \emph{budgeting}---allocating decoder query capacity according to object density---rather than intricate query selection.Motivated by this view, we formulate a monotonic and conservative budgeting principle and propose a budgeting-based DETR (BUTR), a streamlined framework that uses a lightweight, non-learned budgeter to estimate an input-dependent query budget $K(x)$ from encoder confidences. BUTR retains standard Top-$K(x)$ query initialization without additional learned modules or heuristic filtering in the budgeter.At $800\times800$ resolution, BUTR-L achieves 35.7 AP at 47.8 FPS on AI-TOD-v2 and 29.8 AP at 42.1 FPS on VisDrone on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Inference-time integration on COCO further demonstrates its applicability to general scenario detection. Code is available at https://github.com/zhangyi-magic/BUTR.

title: How Robust Are CNNs and Vision Transformers for Alzheimer's MRI Classification Across Datasets?
abstract: Accurate assessment of Alzheimer's disease stages from MRI is important for understanding disease progression and supporting the development of computer-aided analysis tools. Deep learning models have shown promising results for Alzheimer's disease classification from MRI. However, when evaluated on single datasets, it is difficult to determine whether the observed performance reflects consistent architectural behavior or dataset-specific effects. In this work, we present a multi-dataset benchmarking framework with standardized preprocessing and evaluation. We compare five architectures: ResNet-50, ReXNet-150, Swin Transformer, ViT-Base, and ViT-Large. The models are evaluated across three MRI datasets representing severe class imbalance, train-test distribution mismatch, and large-scale augmentation. The results show broadly consistent performance patterns across datasets, with ViT-Large achieving the best performance on all three datasets and reaching up to 99.84% accuracy and 99.86% macro F1. Performance differences between architectures are most pronounced under distribution mismatch and considerably smaller in the augmented-data setting. Across datasets, lower class-level performance is observed primarily among adjacent early-stage categories, particularly Very Mild and Mild impairment. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating deep learning architectures across multiple data conditions rather than relying on single-dataset performance.

title: Smart transfer: Leveraging vision foundation model for rapid building damage mapping with post-earthquake VHR imagery
Continental-scale Sentinel-1 InSAR deformation rate mosaics of central North America
abstract: Ground deformation driven by natural and anthropogenic processes poses significant risks to infrastructure and public safety. Although many regions have been studied, large areas remain poorly characterized because they are remote, sparsely populated, or not expected to experience deformation. Nevertheless, unrecognized natural and anthropogenic processes can produce substantial ground deformation. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides high-resolution, high-precision measurements and enables systematic, cost-effective monitoring over large areas. Here, we present continental-scale ground deformation rate mosaics over central North America, covering the contiguous United States together with adjacent parts of southern Canada and northern Mexico, derived from over 77,000 Sentinel-1 SAR images acquired between 2014 and 2026. The dataset includes both ascending and descending acquisitions, organized into 522 frames and processed using a fully automated workflow and the Multidimensional Small Baseline Subset (MSBAS) software for time-series analysis. Atmospheric phase delays were corrected using a power-law model that also removed long-wavelength signals ( > 20 km), which improved the precision of the remaining short-wavelength signals and placed the resulting rates in a distributed local reference frame. Four mosaics were generated: ascending and descending line-of-sight, and horizontal east-west and vertical deformation components, with corresponding standard error estimates. The high-pass-filtered mosaics, produced at 40 m spatial resolution, reveal spatially coherent deformation patterns, with mean standard errors between 8.9 and 12.6 mm/yr. Temporal coverage is spatially nonuniform, and some signals may reflect processes other than ground deformation. Nonetheless, these products are valuable for identifying new areas of potential concern and guiding site-specific investigations. Several illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate the broad range of detected signals. All datasets are publicly available on Mendeley Data and are expected to support scientific research and regulatory applications.

title: A prototype-based metric-learning model for sea-ice type mapping from Sentinel-1 SAR and ancillary data
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Limited labeled data remains a central challenge for deep-learning-based sea-ice type mapping, while cross-channel relationships remain underexploited, and interaction mechanisms are lacking. This study proposes ESICM, combining Sentinel-1 SAR, AMSR2 brightness temperatures, and ERA5 environmental variables for pixel-level mapping of open water (OW), young ice (YI), first-year ice (FYI), and multi-year ice (MYI). ESICM adopts prototype-based metric learning to fully exploit labels, incorporates a channel multiplication-division module to enhance cross-channel interactions, and introduces two interaction functions, supports-input selection and user dense prompts, to improve classification in hard-to-classify scenes. On the AI4Arctic dataset, trained on 492 AI4Arctic scenes and tested on 20 scenes, ESICM achieved 93.34% overall accuracy, 93.08% F1 score (F1), 88.40% Kappa coefficient, and 77.29% mean intersection over union, exceeding the second-best results by 0.85%–1.55%. Under challenging melt-affected conditions, MYI F1 and intersection over union exceeded the second-best results by 3.13% and 3.93%. Across forward-temporal, cross-region, reduced-training-data, and cross-dataset experiments, ESICM ranked first for 14 and second for two of 16 metrics, indicating relatively strong generalization. In two hard-to-classify scenes, simulated user prompts covering 10% of valid pixels improved all four metrics by more than 4% and 20% over prompt-free inference, respectively, supporting the technical feasibility of interaction. SHAP attributions were broadly consistent with established sea-ice remote-sensing knowledge, enhancing the model’s post hoc interpretability. Overall, ESICM improved sea-ice mapping with limited labeled data and showed application potential under controlled distribution shifts and simulated interaction.

title: UniPoly: A unified instance-level framework for polygon and polyline extraction from remote sensing images
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing

title: Enhancing soil property retrieval in an Ali-Perudic Argosols–dominated region through multi-angle hyperspectral feature integration
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Soil bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) is strongly influenced by soil physicochemical properties, yet most hyperspectral retrieval studies rely on single-view reflectance, leaving the value of multi-angle information insufficiently explored. In this study, bidirectional reflectance factors (BRFs) were measured at 48 viewing angles for 156 soil samples collected from a region dominated by Ali-Perudic Argosols. An optimal multi-angle retrieval framework was developed for different soil properties by systematically comparing spectral preprocessing methods, feature extraction, and modeling algorithms. The effects of viewing angle on retrieval accuracy and feature wavelength distribution were further analyzed, and the applicability of simulated multi-angle BRFs generated using SOILSPECT model was further assessed. Results show that the optimal framework for single-view reflectance combines Savitzky–Golay (SG) smoothing, a hybrid random frog–competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (RFROG–CARS) feature selection strategy, and nonlinear support vector machine (SVM) regression. Retrieval accuracy varied substantially with viewing geometry, and no universal optimal viewing angle was identified across soil properties. For multi-angle BRF data, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN) feature extraction approach outperformed the RFROG–CARS wavelength selection method. Specifically, R 2 (RMSE) improved from 0.64 (8.8 g/kg) to 0.73 (7.7 g/kg) for SOM content, from 0.53 (6.9 %) to 0.61 (6.3 %) for sand content, and from 0.64 (4.7 %) to 0.69 (4.4 %) for silt content, while remaining comparable for cation exchange capacity (0.77/2.4 cmol/kg to 0.76/2.4 cmol/kg) and clay content (0.80/4.3 % to 0.79/4.3 %). Although the retrieval accuracy based on multi-angle BRFs remained slightly lower than that obtained from the optimal viewing geometry, it consistently outperformed most individual viewing angles. The selected multi-angle hyperspectral features were distributed across nearly all viewing angles, indicating complementary spectral–geometric information. Although retrieval accuracy based on simulated BRFs was lower than that based on measured BRFs, the results were broadly comparable. These findings support the use of multi-angle information in soil spectroscopy and remote sensing applications.

title: A physics-constrained superpixel-based multi-source remote sensing spatiotemporal fusion network
abstract: Remote sensing spatiotemporal fusion aims to generate image sequences with both high spatial and temporal resolution. However, many deep learning approaches treat fusion as a black-box regression problem, overlooking differences in sensor imaging physics—such as the point spread function (PSF) and pixel-area integration—which often leads to boundary blurring, spectral mixing, or even physically implausible high-frequency details over heterogeneous landscapes. In addition, these methods commonly rely on paired coarse-/fine-resolution reference images at the same time, which limits data availability. To address these issues, we propose SPP-STF, a superpixel-based fusion network trained with a physics-guided degradation-consistency regularizer that requires only a reference fine-resolution image and a target coarse-resolution observation, while deriving an edge intensity map as a structural prior. The model adopts a U-Net-style, three-branch encoder–decoder to fuse texture, temporal variation, and edge cues at multiple scales. An EdgeResBlock uses high-frequency gating to sharpen boundaries and reduce cross-class leakage, and a superpixel cross-attention Transformer learns object-level correspondences to alleviate alignment errors caused by mixed pixels. During training, we introduce a learnable anisotropic Gaussian PSF-based degradation-consistency term: the predicted fine-resolution output is blurred and downsampled via area integration to match the observed coarse image, and this term is optimized jointly with the reconstruction loss. Quantitatively, SPP-STF achieves the best RMSE, SAM, PSNR, and UIQI on CIA (0.0254, 0.1522, 31.9330 dB, and 0.8451), the best results across all six metrics on LGC (including RMSE 0.0188 and PSNR 34.6307 dB), and the best RMSE, SSIM, SAM, PSNR, and ERGAS on Tianjin (0.0410, 0.7640, 0.2459, 27.8666 dB, and 30.4838). Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of the superpixel and edge modules. The PSF term is interpreted here as a training-time regularizer that provides consistent and physically more reasonable improvements across the three datasets. Structured pruning further indicates that the model can retain spatial structure under substantial compression, while spectral fidelity becomes notably more sensitive beyond roughly 70% pruning.

abstract: The spreading dynamics in social networks are often studied under the assumption that individuals’ statuses, whether informed or infected, are fully observable. However, in many real-world situations, such statuses remain unobservable, which is crucial for determining an individual’s potential to further spread the infection. While final statuses are hidden, intermediate indicators such as symptoms of infection are observable and provide useful representations of the underlying diffusion process. We propose a partial observability-aware Machine Learning framework to infer the parameters of the spreading model. We term the method Distribution Classification, which utilizes the power of classifiers to infer the underlying transmission dynamics. Through extensive benchmarking against likelihood-free inference methods and recent machine learning based baselines, our framework consistently achieves more accurate parameter estimates across diverse diffusion settings while scaling efficiently to large networks. We validate the approach on synthetic networks and demonstrate its applicability to a real-world insider trading network, highlighting its ability to analyze spreading processes when individual states are not directly observable.

title: High-frequency depth distillation from foundation models for multi-view 3D object detection
LLM-augmented temporal knowledge graph reasoning: A dual-view of semantics and structures
Preference Optimization Improves Definition Generation: Semantic Change in EU Institutional Sustainable Finance Disclosures
abstract: Dictionary-like definition generators are known to be useful for lexical semantic change detection (LSCD). However, they suffer from overly granular sense distribution, producing excessive number of definitions for one and the same lexical sense. In this work, we show that fine-tuning with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) helps to overcome this problem. We test our approach both quantitatively on a curated academic LSCD benchmark and qualitatively on real-world data for a practical task of auditing diachronic changes in sustainability terminology within project documentation of EU development finance. All models, code and predictions produced in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/ltgoslo/dpo-for-definition-generation.

title: Graph Spectral Series and Its Signatures
abstract: Bandlimitedness is a central modeling assumption in graph signal processing (GSP), but many graph signals exhibit substantial energy throughout the graph-frequency domain. We introduce a new framework for analyzing such non-bandlimited signals by treating their graph Fourier spectra as ordered sequences and representing them with path signatures. Specifically, motivated by the observation that non-bandlimited graph spectra often display rough, time-series like behavior, we introduce the notion of graph spectral series and develop a signature-based representation that captures global spectral structure without frequency truncation. We establish conditions under which the proposed representation is continuous and characterize its information-preserving properties. We further provide an asymptotic interpretation of graph spectral series for sequences of expanding graphs. Experiments on real-world trend-prediction and change-detection tasks show that signature features can improve performance over representations based directly on the original graph signals. The proposed approach provides a novel principled signature-based tool for analyzing non-bandlimited graph signals.

title: Compression of Vision Foundation Models for Retinal OCT via Growing-Neural-Gas Codebooks and Graph-Guided Masked Image Modeling
abstract: Vision foundation models for retinal imaging are large and computationally demanding, limiting point-of-care deployment. We ask how much of such a model's downstream utility survives compression into a smaller network. We propose a topology-aware discretization framework that distills a continuous foundation model into a discrete codebook, then uses it as the reconstruction target for masked image modeling (MIM). It combines gradient-free codebook learning via Growing Neural Gas, which yields an adjacency graph over the codes, with a graph-distance soft cross-entropy loss that replaces one-hot MIM targets with topologically graded supervision. With student pretraining on 383 public Duke iAMD optical coherence tomography (OCT) volumes, the pipeline distills an 86M-parameter teacher into a 22M-parameter student with at least 3.6x fewer FLOPs. The student performs close to, and in some settings above, its teacher across three classification and two segmentation benchmarks, with the magnitude and direction of the difference depending on the teacher, task, metric, and student capacity. On the external OLIVES benchmark, it surpasses its MIRAGE teacher on every metric (98.06% vs. 95.22% balanced accuracy). It works with two Vision Transformer (ViT-Base) teachers, retinal (MIRAGE) and natural-image (DINOv3); with the out-of-domain teacher, the student outperforms it on retinal-layer segmentation, indicating that the added value of retina-specific pretraining is task-dependent: largest for segmentation, while a general-domain teacher is competitive for classification. These results yield compact retinal models potentially suitable for deployment, transferring across OCT datasets, devices, and clinical tasks, including three datasets not used in the student's pretraining.

title: Exploring Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Representation Learning of Powder X-ray Diffraction Patterns
abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the primary high-throughput method for resolving crystal structures, a cornerstone of materials science. As high-throughput synthesis and self-driving laboratories advance, automated XRD pattern analysis has become vital for accelerating materials discovery. However, traditional matrix factorization methods fail when lattice variations cause non-linear peak shifts. At the same time, supervised learning approaches face a combinatorial explosion when handling multi-phase mixtures. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to learn representation embeddings from 1D diffraction patterns. By optimizing a masked self-prediction loss directly within the latent space, the framework captures high-level crystallographic semantics. Downstream evaluations show that lightweight attentive probes trained on frozen JEPA representations achieve space group classification and lattice parameter estimation accuracy close to much larger supervised vision transformers. Furthermore, latent probing reveals that the learned representation space naturally organizes physical transformations, isolating smooth trajectories for peak broadening. Interestingly, decoding along latent paths between single-phase crystal representations yields realistic multi-phase mixture patterns, demonstrating an emergent continuous structure learned without explicit multi-phase supervision.

title: The kernel mean embedding of a random probability distribution and its principal components
abstract: Given a random probability distribution \(F\), whose realizations are defined on \(\mathbb R^d\), and a kernel \(k\), our aim is to analyze the properties of the kernel mean embedding, \(μ_F\), of \(F\) as a random element of the corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). This establishes a rigorous framework in which kernel statistical techniques for distributional data can be stated both in the sample and population settings and, thus, the asymptotic properties of sample procedures can be properly established. As an illustration of this approach we focus on the principal components of \(F\). We obtain a general convergence result and the explicit expression of the spectral decomposition for the uncentered covariance operator of a normal probability distribution with a Gaussian distributed expectation. The performance of this kernel principal components procedure is illustrated with simulations and the analysis of the intensity distribution in synthetic aperture radar images.

title: Automated identification of ivory carvings using machine learning: A proof-of-concept approach to detecting the illegal wildlife trade
abstract: Despite a ban on the international trading of recently poached ivory, elephants are still killed for their tusks. Ivory and its products are mainly sold in online marketplaces. However, due to the huge volume and variety of adverts and the similarity of ivory with other materials that can be legally sold, it is hard for enforcement officials to identify illicit trading and prosecute sellers. Existing techniques for identifying elephant ivory, such as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and microscopy, can reliably distinguish ivory from other materials, but require physical access to the item and cannot be applied to photographs alone. As a result, these methods are unsuitable for screening the large volume of images posted in online marketplaces, leaving a gap for automated, image-based identification tools. In this proof of concept work, we investigate the potential of machine learning techniques for image analysis to automatically distinguish ivory objects from bone. We employ a semantic segmentation framework using a U-Net architecture with a ResNet34 backbone, leveraging transfer learning on an augmented dataset of 541 original images. Using a dataset of images of ivory and items resembling carved ivory, several models were trialled. On a distinct test set, the classifier achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.81 and an overall classification accuracy of 81% on confident samples. The paper presents the best-performing model as a proof of concept for developing a system that can effectively identify ivory and its products when indicative features of elephant ivory are present in an image. This work provides initial steps towards a machine learning-based framework designed to advise law-enforcement in detecting illegal elephant ivory trade.

title: U-NeXt: General-purpose event detection for neonatal EEG
abstract: We developed U-NeXt, a general framework for neonatal electroencephalography (EEG) event detection based on semantic segmentation. Its convolutional encoder-decoder directly segments individual channels using long input segments to preserve temporal context. A shared architecture and training framework were developed using low-voltage interval, artefact, and seizure datasets containing 51, 98, and 278 neonates, respectively, comprising over 11,000 hours of EEG and 82,000 annotated events. Performance was compared with task-specific ConvNeXt classifiers. For seizure detection, we also evaluated U-NeXt+, trained on an expanded dataset. Both U-NeXt variants and the ConvNeXt baseline were evaluated on two independent held-out seizure datasets, Helsinki and Cork, comprising 130 neonates, with recordings annotated by three experts. U-NeXt improved detection across all three event types, with particular gains in sensitivity for short events. U-NeXt+ achieved Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.862 and 0.891 on Helsinki and Cork, respectively, and improved hourly seizure burden correlations by 30-40% relative to ConvNeXt. U-NeXt+ met the criterion for expert-level performance on both datasets (p < 0.001). In separate computational benchmarks, U-NeXt reduced batch inference time relative to ConvNeXt by 254-fold on a central processing unit and 200-fold on a graphics processing unit. A common segmentation framework improves detection across diverse neonatal EEG event types while substantially reducing inference time. Accurate seizure burden estimates and performance comparable to expert reviewers support its potential use in continuous monitoring and clinical decision support.

title: Consommé: Conditioned Token Merging for Split Inference
abstract: Split inference partitions a Vision Transformer between a resource-constrained edge device and a server. However, transmitting intermediate tokens across the communication channel is costly. Deploying fine-tuned backbones to every endpoint becomes expensive as well. We study token reduction for split inference under a frozen backbone, where only a small adapter is shipped. We observe that the CLS token plays a dual role: it acts as the global summary the receiver needs for classification, and it serves as a signal on which patches to keep. We propose Consommé, a method utilizing both characteristics. There, an information bottleneck compresses the CLS token into a compact latent which is transmitted in place of the full CLS token and conditions a learned patch gate merging patches into exactly $k$ tokens via soft assignment. It reaches any budget in a single step, thus escaping the per-layer cap of bipartite matching (BPM). On DeiT-S/T, it leads all methods at aggressive token budgets and remains operable at shallow splits where BPM cannot operate, while matching fine-tuned methods at gentle budgets at a fraction of their deployment cost.

title: SCDM-HTD: Spectral-Wise Conditional Diffusion Model for Hyperspectral Target Detection
abstract: Hyperspectral target detection (HTD) aims to locate and recognize objects at a fine-grained scale, playing a pivotal role in remote sensing. Despite significant progress, current HTD methods primarily focus on feature comparison while neglecting distribution learning for background-target separation, which can limit detection robustness in practical applications. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a spectral-wise conditional diffusion model that reformulates HTD as a task of generating a detection map. Specifically, we treat background and target confidence scores as training samples and use the corresponding pixel spectra as guiding conditions to capture the distributional discrepancy between background and target through diffusion and denoising. To enhance practical applicability, we propose a lightweight conditional denoising network based on multilayer perceptron to map noisy confidence scores to their ideal counterparts and adopt a deterministic reverse non-Markov chain to skip sampling steps, thereby accelerating the generation process. Furthermore, we introduce a composite loss to improve background-target separation. This loss integrates constrained energy minimization loss to enhance target saliency and suppress the background by maximizing the target response while minimizing average output energy, alongside binary cross-entropy loss to classify background and target using pixel-wise labels. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, with improvements in both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual effects.

title: DriveOSS: Dataset and Benchmark for 3D Anomaly Segmentation and Open-set Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.

title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.

title: Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers
abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.

title: OlmoEarth v1.3: Embeddings
abstract: We make some OlmoEarth embeddings. To do this, we train a new model: OlmoEarth v1.3. OlmoEarth v1.3 is designed to condense multimodal, multitemporal remote sensing data into a single digestible 64 or 128-dimensional vector. OlmoEarth v1.3 produces state-of-the-art embeddings. In addition, OlmoEarth v1.3 is a strong encoder backbone -- competitive with OlmoEarth v1 and v1.2 -- while requiring 18% and 53% of the GPU hours to train, respectively. We use OlmoEarth v1.3 to compute global, annualized 10m embeddings, which we release under the OlmoEarth artifact license.

title: Complementing DINO Features with Image Structure for Part Discovery
abstract: Self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) like DINO encode rich semantics, enabling training-free segmentation of objects from the background and discovery of their parts via feature clustering. This paper focuses on part discovery: partitioning a foreground object into semantic parts. Existing approaches produce imprecise part boundaries. We trace this to the rigid ViT patch grid used in training DINO, where patches straddling boundaries contain pixels from multiple parts. While DINO's invariance-based training could absorb this pixel-level mixing into clean features, experiments with over 26K foreground patches show it does not: boundary-overlapping patches produce features with higher entropy and lower assignment confidence, blurring predicted part boundaries. Rather than make the massive effort of retraining DINO over geometrically coherent regions, an easier approach is to take boundaries directly from a boundary detector, which supplies the geometric information DINO's features lack. Motivated by this, we introduce Part-DINO, a training-free framework that combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with DINO's semantic features. We use the boundaries to partition the image into regions, pool DINO features within each region, and group them to discover parts. Without any training, Part-DINO produces structurally coherent part assignments, outperforming training-free baselines across four standard benchmarks (CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, PartImageNet-Seg) and remaining competitive with weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods.

title: High Resolution Hyperspectral Quantum Infrared Imaging with Undetected Photons
abstract: Quantum sensing in the infrared regime often demands the use of expensive and cryogenically operated detectors. Nonlinear interferometry has paved the way for information transfer from the infrared to the near--infrared or visible regime in various quantum technologies. A particularly interesting application of these interferometers involves spectrally--resolved quantum imaging using undetected photons, enabled by the use of temperature--tunable parametric amplifiers. In this work, we demonstrate spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm using a spontaneous parametric down conversion based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme, registering the attenuation of a zebrafish larva as a biological feasibility test. We characterize and calibrate the interferometer, having achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with a maximum baseline visibility of $\sim 74\%$ in the near--infrared regime. Phase--stepped readout of a grating spectrometer gives a resolving power of $\sim1460$ (from the spectrometer's point spread function) at 1550 nm, and $\sim 730$ from the coherence length, the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons, over an instantaneous spectral window of $\approx 51$ cm$^{-1}$.

title: Representation Learning via Composite Subspace Flow Matching
abstract: Distilling semantic meaning from raw image data remains a challenge in machine learning. Current self-supervised paradigms face a trade-off: joint-embedding architectures produce relevant features by aggressively discarding intra-class variance, irreversibly spatial and reconstruction. Conversely, generative models preserve spatial details but struggle to isolate semantics, as their optimization is dominated by pixel variations. To bridge this divide, we propose composite subspace flow matching (CSFM). Rather than corrupting data with unstructured isotropic noise, CSFM formulates representation learning as the variance-minimizing inversion of a deterministic degradation curriculum across spectral, color, and illumination subspaces. By bounding trajectory variance with hard temporal style truncation, a capacity-constrained encoder is driven to ignore transient style artifacts and encode persistent content. Empirical evaluations across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10 show that CSFM yields competitive discriminative transferability while preserving generative synthesis across both convolutional and vision transformer architectures. By avoiding the collapse pathologies of non-generative methods, CSFM forms a smooth latent space that outperforms standard optimal transport flows on linear probing and few-shot classification, while enabling coherent synthesis and trajectory interpolation. These results confirm that steering the physical dynamics of generative flows offers a scalable paradigm for learning representations that are simultaneously linearly separable and generatively invertible.

title: Robust reinforcement learning multi-baseline phase unwrapping algorithm with JPEG-LS
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Multi-baseline (MB) phase unwrapping (PU) breaks through the limitations of the phase continuity assumption, but existing MBPU algorithms cannot adapt well to noisy environments. A robust reinforcement learning integer programming multi-baseline PU algorithm with JPEG-LS (RL-MBPU) is proposed. First, the cutting plane–pure integer programming cut-selection process is formulated as a sequential reinforcement-learning problem. An efficacy-guided imitation strategy is used to initialize an MBPU-structure-aware single-cut policy, which is further optimized by an actor–critic method using Cut-PAR2-based trajectory returns to reduce the root-node proof cost. Finally, the initial ambiguity number solution is corrected using dynamic median edge detector based on JPEG-LS, and the PU is completed by using the prediction of the left, top, and top-left neighbors of the current pixel and combining it with the local gradient threshold determination. In both simulation and real data experiments, the RL-MBPU algorithm demonstrated stable PU performance, including computational efficiency and noise robustness for interferograms of different sizes. Compared with the minimum-cost flow and cutting plane–pure integer programming algorithms, the RL-MBPU algorithm reduces the root mean square error by approximately 61.2% and 14.5%, respectively, while improving efficiency by approximately 54.1% and 42.4%, respectively. This can further support high-precision interferometric synthetic aperture radar applications.

title: Airborne observatory for high-resolution land surface temperature and spectral emissivity
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The Land surface temperature and emissivity Airborne Observatory System (LAOS) provides land surface temperature (LST) and spectral land surface emissivity (LSE) at very high spatial resolutions (0.5–4 m) and flexible (e.g., intraday) acquisition times. LAOS enables: (i) to map spectral variations in LSE—an inherent property of land surface materials—and (ii) to analyse spatial and temporal variations in LST in relation to land surface processes. Here, we present the scientific rationale for developing the system, the components of the hardware and the processing chain, and retrieval and validation results from an agricultural case study. The LAOS hardware consists of a HyperCam-LW (Telops Inc.), a Fourier transformed infrared spectrometer that operates in the long-wave infrared (7.7–11.5 µm) and an associated airborne platform. The processing chain includes radiometric calibration, generation of ortho -photo mosaics, noise removal, atmospheric correction (AC) and temperature and emissivity separation (TES). Key innovations with respect to previous airborne hyperspectral TIR studies are an improved noise filtering step and a recalibrated minimum emissivity—spectral contrast relationship derived from an extended set of ECOSTRESS spectral library spectra . For demonstrating LAOS’ capacities, an extensive survey campaign was conducted over the Burana Irrigation Consortium area near Modena, Italy, on 13–15 July 2022. Images were acquired at 1- and 4-meter resolution during three times of the day. Raw image tiles were processed to LST and LSE mosaics and compared with ground measurements. Validation was performed over agricultural surfaces – wheat stubble, melon, and water –providing a more surface-type-diverse assessment than previous more urban-focused studies. The LST mosaics show good agreement with the in-situ temperatures across all three surface types (within-class R 2 = 0.52–0.86, RMSE = 2.0–3.2 K, global R 2 = 0.96). LSE maps reveal crisp changes at field boundaries and appear relatively constant over time (i.e., both during a day and across multiple days). Airborne LSE spectra show mostly reasonable agreement with ground measurements and reproduce the overall spectral shape. Spectral emissivity remains largely stable both diurnally and across days (average variability ∼ 1.1 %), indicating consistent retrieval performance at field scale. The results demonstrate that LAOS produces LST and LSE maps with accuracies consistent with previous hyperspectral TIR studies, showcasing its potential to address pressing questions in various fields, including agriculture (e.g., irrigation), forestry (e.g., stress detection), defence (e.g., target detection), and urban studies (e.g., urban heat islands). As a high spatial resolution airborne TIR imager, LAOS can also serve as a demonstrator for upcoming satellite missions, such as LSTM (Land Surface Temperature Monitoring, ESA), TRISHNA (Thermal Infrared Satellite for High-Resolution Applications, CNES & ISRO), and Eagle-TIR (Explorer for Artemis Geology Lunar and Earth, NASA).

title: Multi-evidence-based assessment and selection of nine reconstructed solar-induced fluorescence products over China
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The availability of multiple long-term reconstructed solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) datasets at varying spatiotemporal resolutions provides new opportunities for investigating vegetation dynamics, particularly for estimating gross primary productivity (GPP) and assessing ecosystem responses to environmental stress. Evaluating the consistency and performance of reconstructed SIF (SIFr) products across different land cover types is therefore essential for their effective application in carbon–water cycle studies. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of nine widely used SIFr products (GOSIF, CSIF, RTSIF, LTSIF, HSIF, JJSIF, PKSIF, DSIF, and HCSIF) across China at a spatial resolution of 0.05° and a monthly temporal scale over the period 2007–2016. A multi-source validation framework was employed, integrating tower-based SIF, site-level and gridded GPP, and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index. We found that although all SIFr products exhibited strong agreement in long-term spatial patterns, substantial discrepancies existed in interannual trends. Agreement in long-term mean spatial patterns was generally higher than that in the spatial patterns of temporal trends and varied across land cover types, with stronger agreement observed in grasslands and croplands and lower agreement in forests. Across multiple validation datasets, RTSIF shows comparatively favorable performance, followed by CSIF and GOSIF, which exhibit similar performance. CSIF performs relatively well for GPP but shows lower performance in representing meteorological moisture conditions. Furthermore, product performance exhibits clear land cover dependence, with more reliable results in structurally simple ecosystems and reduced performance in complex canopy environments. We also identified differences in the relative performance of SIFr products across application scenarios and land cover types. These findings highlight the importance of product selection tailored to research objectives and environmental conditions and provide useful information for SIF-based monitoring of vegetation dynamics.

title: Global offshore wind development (2015–2025): multiscale structural evolution based on object-level sar mapping
abstract: Offshore wind is an important renewable infrastructure supporting the global energy transition, making accurate offshore wind turbine (OWT) mapping essential for understanding infrastructure expansion and informing marine spatial management. Existing long-term approaches often extend single-period detections over time based on structural-stability assumptions, but accumulated identification errors and regional imaging differences limit consistent object-level representation across years and regions. To address this challenge, this study proposes a coordinated three-stage object-level SAR mapping framework, in which a stable and balanced sample representation strategy under unified annual temporal windows provides a consistent data basis across regions and years. On this basis, the lightweight YOLO-SAR model integrates frequency-aware feature modeling and hierarchical structural representation to improve OWT detection under heterogeneous conditions. Compared with YOLO11n, YOLO-SAR reduces the parameter count from 2.58 M to 2.30 M while improving mAP@0.5:0.95 from 0.3956 to 0.4553. Spatial reconstruction then transforms detection outputs into consistent annual object-level OWT maps, forming a continuous spatial database covering 2015–2025. Multi-region validation and comparisons with public datasets further support the reliability of these spatial records. These records reveal multiscale patterns of offshore wind spatial evolution: shifts in regional contributions reshape global growth, regional expansion pathways and internal spatial restructuring exhibit stage-dependent differences, and site-boundary expansion and turbine-spacing adjustments determine local spatial organization. These findings demonstrate that global offshore wind development is not merely a process of quantitative growth, but a multiscale spatial evolution driven by regional shifts, site expansion, and internal spatial reorganization. The proposed framework provides a consistent data foundation for global offshore wind evolution analysis and can be extended to other marine energy infrastructures.

title: Quantifying anisotropic impacts of LCZ landscape patterns on NO2 variabilities in the Yangtze River Delta, China
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Urban landscape patterns strongly affect air quality, yet existing studies often neglect anisotropic processes, rely on arbitrary fixed-radius buffers, and lack standardized classification frameworks. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel analytical framework that integrates high-accuracy Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification, multi-scale spatial modeling, and a shape-adaptive influence zone. Central to this framework is the Adaptive Directionally Weighted Sector Influence Zone (ADWSIZ), a new method that explicitly captures the directional heterogeneity of landscape effects on pollutants. Applied to station-based NO 2 measurements in the Yangtze River Delta (YRD) urban agglomeration, we used multi-scale Geographically Weighted Ridge Regression (GWRR) to identify a 4000 m circular buffer as the optimal modeling scale, revealing a clear decoupling from the intrinsic static LCZ pattern scale (approximately 1000 m). Building upon this optimal distance, the ADWSIZ model was developed to refine the influence zone’s shape. The application of ADWSIZ improved model performance (Adjusted R 2 : 0.464 → 0.506 ; RMSE: 2.950 → 2.834 µg/m 3 ) and reduced residual spatial autocorrelation. Our findings highlight that the anisotropic influence of features like industrial land and compact high-rise fabrics is a critical, previously underexplored factor in explaining NO 2 variation. This study establishes a replicable and transferable methodology that advances the conceptualization of influence zones from simple distance-based buffers to scale- and shape-adaptive forms, offering a robust tool for refining spatial coupling analyses between urban morphology and air pollutants.

title: Large-scale building instance segmentation in diverse urban scenes based on LiDAR data
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Building 3D profiles constitute critical factors in urban environmental analyses, including assessments of urban heat island effects, carbon emissions, population distribution, and related challenges. LiDAR data provide comprehensive high-resolution 3D information, enabling the acquisition of detailed 3D building profiles. However, in dense urban environments, buildings are in diverse shapes and heights, and are close to one another, making it challenging to extract building instances. In this paper, we propose BuildGroup, a novel building instance segmentation model for both Airborne Laser Scanning (ALS)-based and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) datasets. It employs the progressive learning strategy in the feature aggregation, which uses prior 2D knowledge from the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to infer spatial relationships within point clouds and mitigate cross-source discrepancies. An offset enhancement module is introduced to mitigate the effects of diverse point densities, improving instance clustering by compacting point cloud distributions. Additionally, an edge-enhanced loss function prioritizes boundary point accuracy during training to enhance morphological precision. Furthermore, we present a building LiDAR dataset with instance-level building information, which fills a key gap in real-world, large-scale urban point cloud segmentation, particularly for ALS-based sparse façade data. Experimental results validate the framework’s capability to produce accurate building instance information across varying urban densities. All code and data are available at https://github.com/littlebeen/BuildGroup .

title: An interpretable DM-PINN for retrieving mangrove canopy carbon, nitrogen, and potassium contents using Sentinel-2 and SDGSAT-1 observations along China's southeastern coast
abstract: Mangroves are among the most important blue carbon ecosystems, contributing substantially to global carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation. Canopy carbon (CCC), nitrogen (CNC), and potassium (CKC) contents provide critical indicators of nutrient cycling, ecosystem functioning, and ecological health. However, the structural complexity and strong spatial heterogeneity of mangroves present major obstacles to understanding the spectral response mechanisms and achieving reliable large-scale retrieval of these biochemical parameters. To address these limitations, we developed an interpretable retrieval framework that integrates causal analysis with physical constraints for reliable estimation of mangrove biochemical parameters. First, we proposed a Multi-Channel Chatterjee-Enhanced Correlation Spectrum Analysis (MC-ξ-CS) method that integrates causal discovery to systematically identify spectral bands causally associated with CCC, CNC, and CKC. For large-scale retrieval of mangrove canopy parameters, the identified causal relationships were transferred to satellite observations through a Global Angle-Divergence Spectral Transfer (GADT) framework, yielding robust estimation (R2 = 0.511–0.669). Subsequently, a Dual-Mechanism Guided Physics-Informed Neural Network (DM-PINN) was developed to synergistically integrate causal analysis and physical constraints, achieving robust retrieval performance (R2 = 0.604–0.83) for three representative mangrove species and enhancing the physical interpretability of the results. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first comprehensive large-scale retrieval of key mangrove biochemical parameters along the southeastern coast of China, revealing CCC values of 409.18–566.89 g/kg (C/N = 9.77–14.21), CNC values of 14.38–74.9 g/kg (N/K = 1.99–3.86), and CKC values of 4.78–19.67 g/kg (C/K = 28.22–37.67). Distinct inter-provincial spatial patterns were observed: CNC and CKC exhibited similar gradients, increasing from landward to seaward regions, whereas CCC displayed an opposite spatial distribution pattern with lower values in coastal regions. Moreover, CCC was strongly positively correlated with CNC, while CKC showed negative correlations with both parameters. Collectively, this study established a novel theoretical and methodological framework for elucidating the spectral response mechanisms of mangrove biochemical parameters, offering critical scientific support for large-scale mangrove degradation monitoring, ecological restoration assessment, and biodiversity conservation.

title: Wavelet-guided decomposition of two-dimensional InSAR time series: insights into long-term settlement and cyclic deformation of a high earth-rockfill dam
abstract: Long-term deformation of high earth-rockfill dams reflects post-construction consolidation, creep, reservoir loading, and cyclic operation. Separating these superimposed components is essential for gaining process-level insights into spatial patterns and differential responses. This study investigates the Pubugou Dam, a 186 m high earth-rockfill dam in Southwest China, using ascending and descending Sentinel-1 observations from 2017–2023. The two viewing geometries were jointly inverted to recover vertical and east-west displacements. A wavelet-guided decomposition, in which dominant periods identified by the continuous wavelet transform constrain the window length and component grouping in singular spectrum analysis, was proposed to separate the displacement records into long-term trend, annual cyclic, and residual components. Synthetic experiments yielded root mean square errors of 0.69–2.16 mm, indicating effective decomposition performance. Cross wavelet transform and wavelet transform coherence quantified localized coherence and phase lags between the cyclic components and reservoir water level. The central earth-rockfill body exhibits the largest magnitudes of vertical and east-west deformation rates, whereas the spillway and abutments remained comparatively stable. The trend components and settlement indices are consistent with relatively slow long-term post-construction settlement during the observation period. Annual cyclic deformation is more pronounced in the east-west direction and exhibits spatially variable lags relative to reservoir level fluctuations. Settlement inclination and apparent horizontal strain remain low under the adopted criteria, suggesting limited crest-cracking susceptibility during the observation period. This work demonstrates how wavelet-guided decomposition of two-dimensional InSAR time series provides spatially explicit insights into long-term settlement and cyclic deformation of high earth-rockfill dams.

title: Learning Complex Scene Segmentation from Noisy Label
SkinTokens : A Learned Compact Representation for Unified Autoregressive Rigging
abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative 3D models has created a critical bottleneck in animation pipelines: rigging. Existing automated methods are fundamentally limited by their approach to skinning, treating it as an ill-posed, high-dimensional regression task that is inefficient to optimize and is typically decoupled from skeleton generation. We posit this is a representation problem and introduce SkinTokens : a learned, compact, and discrete representation for skinning weights. By leveraging an FSQ-CVAE to capture the intrinsic sparsity of skinning, we reframe the task from continuous regression to a more tractable token sequence prediction problem. This representation enables TokenRig , a unified autoregressive framework that models the entire rig as a single sequence of skeletal parameters and SkinTokens, learning the complicated dependencies between skeletons and skin deformations. The unified model is then amenable to a reinforcement learning stage, where tailored geometric and semantic rewards improve generalization to complex, out-of-distribution assets. Quantitatively, the SkinTokens representation leads to a 98%–133% relative improvement in skinning-weight L 1 error over state-of-the-art methods, while the full TokenRig framework, refined with RL, improves the skeletal Chamfer distance by 17%–22% . Our work presents a unified, generative approach to rigging that yields higher fidelity and robustness, offering a scalable solution to a long-standing challenge in 3D content creation.

Development and validation of a red-edge-based index for improving satellite detection of algal blooms in inland waters
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The increasing frequency of freshwater algal blooms threatens aquatic ecosystems globally. While remote sensing algorithms are widely used for bloom detection, conventional methods frequently exhibit degraded performance under optically complex conditions (e.g., sunglint, thin clouds, and high turbidity) and lack sensitivity to sparse blooms. To address these limitations, this study introduces the Red-Edge Floating Algae Index (RFAI). Structured as a baseline-height model, the RFAI mathematically isolates the scattering-induced spectral curvature of algal blooms using three critical Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) bands: the green reflectance peak (∼560 nm), the red absorption trough (∼665 nm), and the red-edge reflectance peak (∼704 nm). This formulation effectively decouples genuine target signals from confounding background noise. Comparative validation against 17 widely used indices across a diverse set of inland lakes demonstrated the statistically significant overall effectiveness of the RFAI ( p < 0.0001), yielding precision and F1-score improvements of up to 42.8 % and 26.6 %, respectively, under locally optimized parameterizations. Crucially, the RFAI demonstrates robust comprehensive stability across highly variable, optically challenging conditions, effectively mitigating the severe performance fluctuations often observed in individual conventional indices. Supported by a novel optical-type-stratified thresholding strategy, the RFAI establishes a scalable and versatile framework for operational bloom monitoring using compatible red-edge satellite systems, enabling the generation of reliable observational records essential for the sustainable management of aquatic ecosystems.

title: Reconstructing multi-temporal Glacier area changes to improve mass balance estimates in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau (2000–2025)
abstract: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP), a critical component of the “Asian Water Tower”, hosts a large concentration of maritime temperate glaciers that are highly sensitive to climate change. However, persistent cloud cover, seasonal snow, and supraglacial debris complicate consistent long-term glacier mapping, while the use of static glacier boundaries may introduce temporal mismatches in altimetry-based glacier mass-change estimates. In this study, we developed a multi-source data-fusion framework on Google Earth Engine (GEE) to reconstruct glacier-area changes in the SETP from 2000 to 2025 at five-year intervals and 30 m spatial resolution. Random Forest classifiers were used to integrate Landsat and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 synthetic-aperture-radar data, and NASADEM-derived topographic information, supporting glacier delineation under complex surface and atmospheric conditions. The reconstructed glacier area decreased from 8,083 ± 664 km2 in 2000 to 6,228 ± 572 km2 in 2025, corresponding to a cumulative loss of 22.9 ± 3.6% and a mean loss rate of 80.51 ± 10.51 km2 yr−1. The mean area-loss rates were 51.31 ± 6.51 km2 yr−1 during 2000–2010 and 92.99 ± 15.55 km2 yr−1 during 2010–2025, indicating a higher average loss rate in the later period. By combining satellite-altimetry-derived elevation changes from ICESat, CryoSat-2, and ICESat-2 with the reconstructed time-varying glacier areas, we estimated a mean glacier mass-change rate of −6.51 ± 1.22 Gt yr−1 during 2003–2022. Compared with using a fixed 2003 glacier area, the time-varying-area calculation reduced the estimated mass-loss magnitude by 0.63 Gt yr−1, equivalent to 8.8% of the fixed-area estimate. These results indicate that incorporating time-varying glacier areas can reduce temporal mismatch in altimetry-based mass-change estimation and improve the temporal consistency of regional glacier mass-change assessments.

title: A Metro-InSAR Risk Index for corridor-scale displacement risk diagnosis of urban rail infrastructure
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Time-series Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides dense displacement observations along urban rail corridors, yet converting point-based measurements into corridor-scale diagnostic information remains challenging. This study proposes the Metro-InSAR Risk Index (MIRI), a diagnostic index designed to convert multi-dimensional InSAR-derived displacement characteristics into displacement-related diagnostic levels for urban metro corridors. MIRI integrates displacement rate, cumulative displacement, local displacement heterogeneity, height-related variability, and temporal residual variability, thereby extending conventional velocity-based interpretation toward corridor-scale displacement-risk diagnosis. The framework was applied to the Kunming Metro Network using 198 descending Sentinel-1 images acquired from March 2018 to December 2024. The time-series InSAR results show that the network was generally stable, with line-of-sight (LOS) displacement rates mainly ranging from −6 to 3 mm/yr and 97.21% of coherent scatterers falling within the stable interval of −3 to 3 mm/yr. Localized displacement anomalies were mainly observed near line intersections, curved sections, construction-affected areas, and the Dianchi Lake shoreline. Based on MIRI, 78%, 17%, 4%, and 1% of valid points were classified as Levels D, C, B, and A, respectively, indicating a distribution dominated by lower diagnostic levels, with spatially confined Level-B and Level-A anomalies particularly along Lines 4 and 5 and in lakeside soft-ground areas. Multi-source contextual variables and XGBoost-SHAP analysis were further used to interpret the environmental, anthropogenic, operational, and displacement-gradient information associated with the MIRI-based diagnostic patterns. The results indicate that the spatial variation in MIRI is mainly associated with terrain-related conditions, corridor-scale displacement variation, metro operation, and urban development intensity. By deriving diagnostic levels directly from PSI-based displacement indicators, MIRI provides an InSAR-based screening tool for prioritizing displacement-related anomalies and supporting maintenance of urban rail transit systems.

Second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling for spatial prediction
abstract: Spatial prediction is a fundamental task in geographic information science and environmental resource assessment. However, under complex terrain and heterogeneous covariates, models relying only on point-scale attributes or a single global relationship often have difficulty representing spatial context and regional heterogeneity. This study proposes a second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling framework (SDA-SCA) that integrates first-dimension covariates, neighborhood-based second-dimension features, covariate screening, spatially constrained stratification, and local model training. Using two independently constructed annual spatial-prediction cases based on surface solar radiation observations from 670 stations in China in 2022 and 2023, five modeling schemes—Ordinary Kriging, Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF), first-dimension attribute modeling (FDA), second-dimension augmented modeling (SDA), and SDA-SCA—were evaluated under spatial cross-validation. SDA-SCA showed a consistent predictive advantage across the two independent annual cases and the three evaluated model families. Relative to FDA, SDA-SCA increased R2 by 0.11–0.16 in 2022 and 0.17–0.21 in 2023, while reducing RMSE by 12.4%–17.7% and 24.3%–33.7%, and MAE by 22.8%–35.5% and 31.5%–50.4%, respectively. Stage-wise ablation showed that the FDA-to-SDA step produced consistent but moderate improvements, whereas the SDA-to-SDA-SCA step provided larger and more stable gains. These results indicate that second-dimension features improve the representation of neighborhood context, and their predictive value is further strengthened when coupled with spatial stratification. SHAP analysis further confirmed the substantial contribution of second-dimension features to the integrated model. The proposed framework provides an extensible pathway for spatial prediction tasks requiring the joint representation of local attributes, neighborhood context, and spatial heterogeneity.
